info.bio:
The Lords of the Underground (L.O.T.U.G.) is a hip-hop trio based in Newark, New Jersey. MCs Mr. Funke and DoItAll Dupré met DJ Lord Jazz (a native of Cleveland) when all three were undergraduates at Shaw University[citation needed]. Fellow New Jersey rapper Redman served as one of the group's early DJ's.

The group released their debut album, Here Come the Lords on March 9, 1993 with production handled by Marley Marl and K-Def. The album peaked at 66 on the Billboard 200 and featured five charting singles

scenes.name: Nueva Jersey: Flavor Unit, Redman, Lords of the Underground y los Fugees
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Desde Sugar Hill, Nueva Jersey pesó en el hip hop: la Flavor Unit de Mark the 45 King (Queen Latifah, Chill Rob G, Lakim Shabazz); Latifah convenció a los New Style de East Orange de llamarse Naughty by Nature. Luego vino una segunda ola: Redman (aliado de EPMD), Lords of the Underground (DoItAll, Mr. Funke y DJ Lord Jazz, de la Universidad de Shaw, producidos por Marley Marl en su «House of Hits»), Artifacts, Das EFX, Outsidaz y Rah Digga; Just Blaze pinchaba sus propias bases en las noches de micro abierto del Pipeline de Newark. Casi todos entraron aliándose con grupos de Nueva York. Los Fugees (Wyclef Jean, Lauryn Hill, Pras) mezclaron reggae, rap y R&B con instrumentos en Ruffhouse: Blunted on Reality (1994) y The Score (1996), Grammy al mejor disco de rap, con «Fu-Gee-La» (una base que Fat Joe rechazó), «Killing Me Softly» y «Ready or Not»: Lauryn Hill, entre las mejores MCs de la historia.

scenes.name: Rap de la Costa Oeste y G-funk
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La Costa Oeste fue desde el principio terreno de rap funk: Uncle Jamm’s Army de Rodger Clayton y Egyptian Lover, con disfraces a lo P-Funk y electro-funk desde 1981; Too Short en Oakland, pionero del rap X y de la fusión con bajo real («I Wanna Be Free», con Shorty B). Pero el sonido que arrasó vino del sur de Los Ángeles: N.W.A. (Ice Cube, Dr. Dre, Eazy-E, Yella) y «Straight Outta Compton» (1989), misoginia y rabia, fantasías de agresión contra un sistema que no cede («Fuck tha Police»). Con la apatía de Bush, el crack y las armas, el encarcelamiento de James Brown y la humillación de los ídolos, Ice Cube predijo en Death Certificate (1991) la revuelta de Rodney King de 1992; el hip hop estaba mejor informado que la prensa. Cuando los pleitos encarecieron los samples, Dr. Dre y Snoop volvieron a tocar con músicos: The Chronic (1993). En 1995 el funk estaba en todos los títulos: The G Funk Era de Warren G, Funkdafied de Da Brat, Guerrilla Funk de Paris. «El hip hop salvó el funk», dijo Clinton; ahora le toca al funk salvar al hip hop.

mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …time I heard “Rapper’s Delight.” And I memorized it. Every word, every line in reverse, I just fell in love with it. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): There was the relatable lines. If you talking about fried chicken in the Black and Brown neighborhood, when you talking about it tastes like wood,…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …and life in the urban communities. And to this day, I think that’s one of the best-written rap songs in history. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): We didn’t recognize the power of it being a mainstream thing. We did understand that it brought our communities together. We did understand that…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …to change its name from the New Style to Naughty by Nature. Soon a new generation of dynamic New Jersey artists surfaced, which included Redman, Lords of the Underground, the Fugees, Artifacts, and Rah Digga of the New Jersey collective Outsidaz. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): Before I got with Lords of the Underground, Redman was my DJ and we had a crew with a bunch of other guys from New Jersey, and we used to call ourselves Revolutionary Party of Terrace, RPT.…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …met while at North Carolina’s Shaw University, eventually attracting the attention of legendary producer Marley Marl. Marl produced the bulk of the Lords of the Underground’s 1993 debut album, Here Come the Lords, which included hits like “Chief Rocka” and “Funky Child.” Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): We came up to his house, just to be standing outside the garage door, hearing this vibration of music and for Marley to say, “Welcome to the House…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …it’s like that second wave of Jersey artists. First you had the Flavor Unit: Latifah, the 45 King. And then you have this next generation: Redman, Lords of the Underground, the Outsidaz. [Dray] from Das EFX is from Teaneck. There was an open mic that used to happen in Newark at a club called the Pipeline. And this was…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …Tame from the Artifacts decides to jump up on stage during the open mic. Or Redman shows up or Young Zee from the Outsidaz shows up. Or DoItAll from Lords of the Underground shows up. And I’m the one DJing. And a lot of times I’m playing my own beats off of a tape. Artists that I look up to are asking to freestyle on…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …in a sense. These mythical beings, they’re all of a sudden right in front of you, rhyming on one of your tracks. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): You had all of those Jersey crews in the ’90s from Queen Latifah to Apache to Naughty by Nature to Redman, Lords of the Underground, Rah Digga, the Artifacts. Even though it was hard for us to break in, most of the New Jersey acts, we broke in by teaming up

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: with New York crews. Lords of the Underground, Marley Marl. That’s the House of Hits and everybody came to that house, from Heavy D to LL Cool J to TLC. And then you had Redman, who teamed up…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …talk shit to you in the singing type of voice until you’re like, Man, this motherfucker cursed me out singing to me. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): We were in Florida on Tupac’s tour. It was Lords of the Underground. Outkast was opening up. I think it was six groups in three vans, and Lords and Pac used to chill. He would come to my room and we would build. Even…

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …and the art form as a means of enlightenment and education, versus it being a vessel for pure entertainment. Dupré “DoItAll” Kelly (artist, Lords of the Underground): When I think about hip-hop, I look at it this way. Break the word down. “Hip” is being in the know, right? “Hop” is a form of movement. That’s why…

mentions.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
mentions.author: Rickey Vincent
mentions.text: …of rappers came with funk themes in their album titles: Warren G was in The G Funk Era, Da Brat was Funkdafied, Goldie was In the Land of Funk, the Lords of the Underground were Keepers of the Funk, political rapper Paris delivered Guerilla Funk, and it keeps on coming. The Funk is now the central focus in higher forms…
